title: Hindu-Muslim shared saints (Kabir, the Sufis of the Deccan) — taught as history
hook: Ram and Allah, guru and pir: a poet keeps both sets of words, side by side
carry: Hindu-Muslim shared saints (Kabir, the Sufis of the Deccan) — taught as history
tomorrow: if God's not in the temple or the mosque, then where?

segments.voice: Yesterday, Hindu-Muslim shared saints began with Kabir: a weaver whose songs both sides kept, and half the flowers each. Today, the names he used for God.

A couple sits down to dinner. She grew up saying Bhagwan. He grew up saying Allah. Their little girl has just asked who God is, and both parents are waiting to see who answers first. Which word goes on that table? A poet faced his own version of it. Ram. Allah. Hari. Karim. Guru. Pir. In one song credited to Kabir, all of these sit within a few lines of each other. A listener from the temple and a listener from the mosque could each hear a word from home. That isn't a muddle. It's a choice.
screen: `BHAGWAN OR ALLAH AT DINNER?` → `A SONG WITH BOTH SETS OF NAMES.`

segments.voice: Here's the song, in paraphrase, from the English version Tagore made. Hari is in the east, Allah is in the west. Look in your heart, and there you'll find both Karim and Ram. And it ends: Kabir is the child of Allah and of Ram. He is my guru, he is my pir. Listen to that last pair. Guru is the Hindu word for a spiritual teacher. Pir is the Sufi word for one. Kabir doesn't pick. He doesn't coin a third word that swallows both. He keeps them side by side, each in its own language. A couplet credited to him says it more sharply, again in paraphrase: the Hindu says Ram is dear to me, the Turk says Rahim; the two fought and died, and neither knew the secret. In these songs, Turk means a Muslim. Taught as history, that explains a lot. People could hear Kabir in their own words. A Hindu singer could stay with Ram and Hari. A Muslim listener could stay with Allah and Karim. Both could claim him, because he had spoken to each in its own tongue. So what does it give that couple at dinner? Not a rule. A pattern: each name kept whole, in its own tongue, on the same table.
screen: `HARI EAST, ALLAH WEST.` · `MY GURU, MY PIR.` · `NO THIRD WORD THAT SWALLOWS BOTH.` · then, large: `EACH NAME KEPT WHOLE.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind someone whose word for the sacred is different from yours: a friend, a coworker, someone in your own family. Hold their face for a few breaths, and say their name quietly. If you'd like, send them a short note of thanks for something real, no theology needed.

howItsDone: Kabir's songs, with Ram and Hari beside Allah and Karim, are sung in Hindu devotional settings and remembered by Muslims too; some interfaith families draw on them when each partner's words for God differ.
